correctness.rationale: For Q5, a fort is a nonempty set F with no outside vertex having exactly one F-neighbor. The exact min-fort classification gives minimum size five and precisely the 32 open neighborhoods, reproduced by exhaustive evaluation of all 242,824 subsets of sizes 1–5. Open neighborhoods N(u),N(v) intersect iff centers are at Hamming distance two; same-parity centers must have distance four and at most two such centers per parity, hence rho^o(Q5)≤4, with centers 0,1,30,31 attaining four. An eight-vertex fort {6,7,10,11,20,21,24,25} disjoint from those neighborhoods gives five forts. Six forts require exactly four size-five neighborhoods plus two size-six forts and cover all 32 vertices. For two selected vertices of one parity, at least six opposite-parity vertices have unique adjacency, excluding mixed 6-fort parity counts 2,4; for three selected same-parity vertices a triple-intersection count leaves at least six opposite-parity vertices uniquely adjacent, excluding 3,3. Thus each size-six fort has parity profile (0,6),(1,5),(5,1),(6,0). Mixed profiles contain N(u), giving a forbidden fifth disjoint neighborhood. Every remaining six-vertex monochromatic residual set fails the fort test: an opposite-parity vertex at distance two from the two same-parity centers has exactly one residual neighbor. Independent exhaustive checks verified all 906,192 size-six subsets, 1,600 four-center open packings, residual obstructions, the witness, and Q1–Q4 boundary cases. Q1 is an exceptional opposite-direction inequality ft(Q1)=1<rho^o(Q1)=2; the FINAL repaired slogan correctly limits first strict POSITIVE gap to d≥2. No statement for d>5 or infinite dimension is implied by the finite checks.
